content: 1. Levonorgestrel, when administered via an intrauterine device (IUD), is a contraceptive method approved by the FDA for use in women, particularly those experiencing heavy menstrual bleeding. 2. Common side effects associated with the use of levonorgestrel IUDs include menstrual irregularities, nausea, lower abdominal pain, fatigue, headache, and dizziness. 3. The Mirena IUD is indicated for intrauterine contraception for up to five years. It is also approved for the treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding in women who choose intrauterine contraception as their preferred method. 4. Mirena is recommended for women who have had at least one child. The device should be replaced after five years if continued use is desired. 5. The Mirena system contains 52 mg of levonorgestrel, which is initially released at a rate of approximately 20 mcg per day. This release rate gradually decreases to about half of the initial value after five years. 6. The device is packaged in a sterile inserter, and healthcare providers are advised to thoroughly familiarize themselves with the insertion instructions before attempting to place the device. 7. Mirena should be inserted by a trained healthcare provider within seven days of the onset of menstruation or immediately following a first-trimester abortion, following the provided insertion guidelines. 8. A new Mirena device can be inserted at any time during the menstrual cycle, provided pregnancy has been ruled out. 9. Patients should be counseled on what to expect following Mirena insertion, including potential changes in bleeding patterns during the first few months of use. 10. Analgesics may be prescribed if necessary to manage discomfort associated with insertion. 11. Patients should be reexamined and evaluated 4 to 12 weeks after insertion and then annually, or more frequently if clinically indicated. 12. Removal of the Mirena device should be performed by applying gentle traction on the threads with forceps. The arms of the device will fold upward as it is withdrawn from the uterus. 13. Mirena should not remain in the uterus for more than five years. Removal may be associated with some pain, bleeding, or neurovascular episodes. 14. If the threads are not visible and the device is confirmed to be in the uterine cavity, removal may require the use of narrow forceps, such as alligator forceps, and may necessitate cervical dilation. 15. 16. If Mirena is removed mid-cycle and the patient has had intercourse within the preceding week, there is a risk of pregnancy unless a new Mirena is inserted immediately following removal. 17. If a patient with regular cycles wishes to switch to a different contraceptive method, Mirena should be removed during the first seven days of the menstrual cycle, and the new method should be initiated immediately. 18. For patients with irregular cycles or amenorrhea, or if Mirena is removed after the seventh day of the menstrual cycle, the new contraceptive method should be started at least seven days before removal. 19. There is limited information regarding off-label use of levonorgestrel IUDs in both adult and pediatric patients. 20. Women who become pregnant while using Mirena should be evaluated for ectopic pregnancy, as up to half of pregnancies occurring with Mirena in place are ectopic. 21. Women with a history of ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery, or pelvic infection are at a higher risk of ectopic pregnancy. 22. If pregnancy occurs with Mirena in place, the device should be removed. However, removal or manipulation of the device may result in pregnancy loss. 23. In cases where pregnancy continues with Mirena in place, the patient should be closely monitored and advised of the risks, including miscarriage, sepsis, premature labor, and premature delivery. 24. Long-term effects on offspring when pregnancy continues with Mirena in place are unknown. 25. Congenital anomalies have been reported infrequently in live births following Mirena use, with no clear trend toward specific anomalies. 26. 27. Group A streptococcal sepsis (GAS) has been reported in rare cases following Mirena insertion, with severe pain occurring within hours and sepsis developing within days. 28. Aseptic technique during Mirena insertion is essential to minimize the risk of infection. 29. Mirena is contraindicated in women with known or suspected pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) or a history of PID unless there has been a subsequent intrauterine pregnancy. 30. Women at increased risk of PID, such as those with multiple sexual partners or whose partners have multiple sexual partners, should be counseled on the risks associated with IUD use. 31. Irregular bleeding during the first months of Mirena use may mask symptoms of endometrial polyps or cancer. Persistent or uncharacteristic bleeding should prompt diagnostic evaluation to rule out endometrial pathology. 32. Amenorrhea develops in approximately 20% of Mirena users by one year. If menstruation does not occur within six weeks of the previous cycle, pregnancy should be considered.
